blocks.title: Why Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo matters in a real product

spans.text: Problem statement:

A team is dealing with a release changes the refund-policy prompt and must prove old behavior still works. They do not need trivia about Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo; they need a decision they can make, a concrete artifact they can inspect, and a way to know whether known behaviors preserved after prompt edits is improving.

This lesson keeps one running case in view: Promptfoo regression pack with assertions and release gates. Every module asks what the system sees, what it changes, what can go wrong, and how a reviewer would prove the behavior before trusting it.

Before reading on, predict: if the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases, which part of the design would you inspect first - input, mechanism, decision rule, implementation, or monitoring?
Because this is an intermediate lesson, assume the vocabulary is learnable and spend your effort on tradeoffs, integration points, and the tests that prove the design works.

spans.text: The team reviews Promptfoo regression pack with assertions and release gates after a week of prototype use. One user-visible metric is improving: known behaviors preserved after prompt edits. But a reviewer finds the known failure pattern: the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases.

The decision is not to throw away the prototype. The team keeps the working slice, then adds one missing control: better state capture, stricter retrieval, a clearer schema, a human approval step, or a monitoring alert depending on the failure.

items.text: What changed: the artifact now records the evidence it used, not just the final answer.

spans.text: The happy path for Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo is not enough. In the running case, watch for failures that look successful until a user, auditor, or downstream system checks the details.

items.text: Silent success: the system returns an answer or artifact but hides that evidence was missing, stale, or incomplete.
Wrong abstraction: the team optimizes a model, framework, or metric when the real problem is data quality, policy, state, or workflow ownership.
Evaluation gap: tests cover polished examples but not the known failure case: the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases.
Operational drift: the design works once, then degrades when traffic, data, users, or dependencies change.

blocks.title: Runnable check: turn a golden case into a release gate
blocks.code:
# Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo: minimal eval gate.
golden = {
    "id": "refund-policy-1",
    "must_include": ["30 days", "invoice id"],
    "must_not_include": ["guaranteed approval"],
}
answer = "Refund requests need the invoice id and must arrive within 30 days."

def passes(case, answer):
    lower = answer.lower()
    has_required = all(term.lower() in lower for term in case["must_include"])
    avoids_forbidden = all(term.lower() not in lower for term in case["must_not_include"])
    return has_required and avoids_forbidden

print(golden["id"])
print("pass" if passes(golden, answer) else "fail")

spans.text: This is not the full production implementation of Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo. It is a runnable miniature that makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision, output, and a check tied to the running failure mode.

questions.why: The lesson is valuable only if it changes an artifact, release gate, or evaluation tied to known behaviors preserved after prompt edits.
questions.rot: Prefer the smallest design that exposes the failure case: the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct Prompt Regression Testing with promptfoo as a five-part path: the concrete problem (a release changes the refund-policy prompt and must prove old behavior still works), the mechanism, the design choice, the implementation or verification check, and the failure mode (the new prompt passes happy paths but fails refusal and citation cases). Then name the metric that tells you whether the work improved: known behaviors preserved after prompt edits.
